claim: Myotubularin related protein-2 (Mtmr2) was identified as a significantly enriched member of the native Piezo2 interactome in murine dorsal root ganglia (DRG) with a p-value of 0.00030 and an enrichment factor of log2 9.96.
source: Our previous work revealed Mtmr2 as a highly enriched member of the native Piezo2 interactome in DRG (significance of identification: p=0.00030, unpaired t-test; enrichment factor: log2 9.96) (Narayanan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a previous interactomics screen (Narayanan et al., 2016) with specific statistical values provided.

claim: Mtmr2 is expressed in peripheral sensory neurons of DRG including those neurons expressing Piezo2.
source: We first validated the reported expression of Mtmr2 in peripheral sensory neurons of DRG (Previtali et al., 2003; Vaccari et al., 2011) including those neurons expressing Piezo2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b and citations to previous literature (Previtali et al., 2003; Vaccari et al., 2011).

claim: Piezo2 and Mtmr2 are in close vicinity in both somata and neurites of cultured DRG neurons as demonstrated by proximity ligation assay (PLA).
source: In this way we could show the close vicinity of Piezo2 and Mtmr2 in both, somata and neurites of cultured DRG neurons, and upon co-transfection in HEK293 cells (Figure 1a–d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1a-d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Mtmr2 overexpression suppresses Piezo2-mediated RA-MA currents in HEK293 cells compared to mock transfection.
source: Interestingly, Mtmr2 co-expression led to a pronounced reduction of Piezo2-mediated RA-MA currents compared to mock conditions (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: The displacement threshold of Piezo2 RA-MA currents is significantly increased upon Mtmr2 overexpression in HEK293 cells.
source: Moreover, the displacement threshold of RA-MA currents was significantly increased upon Mtmr2 overexpression indicating the requirement of stronger mechanical stimulation to reach a threshold current amplitude (Supplementary file 1; please see Materials and methods for details on the calculation of the displacement threshold) (Eijkelkamp et al., 2013; Morley et al., 2016; Narayanan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and references to methods used in previous studies (Eijkelkamp et al., 2013; Morley et al., 2016; Narayanan et al., 2016).

claim: The inactivation time constant of Piezo2 currents remains unchanged upon Mtmr2 co-expression in HEK293 cells.
source: Importantly, the inactivation time constant of Piezo2 currents remained unchanged upon Mtmr2 co-expression (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mtmr2 overexpression does not affect Kv1.1 voltage-gated currents in HEK293 cells.
source: To exclude that Mtmr2 overexpression renders cells unhealthy and might therefore unspecifically suppress Piezo2 currents, we co-expressed Mtmr2 with Kv1.1 and measured voltage-gated currents, which were similar to mock transfected controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Mtmr2 overexpression does not modulate Piezo1-mediated MA currents in HEK293 cells.
source: Remarkably, we did not observe any differences in Piezo1 currents upon overexpression of Mtmr2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mtmr2 overexpression suppresses native RA-MA currents in cultured DRG neurons compared to mock transfection.
source: Similar to HEK293 cells, Mtmr2 overexpression suppressed native RA-MA currents in DRG cultures when compared to mock transfection (Figure 1g,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1g,h.

claim: The displacement threshold of RA-MA currents is unaffected upon Mtmr2 overexpression in DRG neurons.
source: The displacement threshold was unaffected upon Mtmr2 overexpression (Supplementary file 1), which is in contrast to our results in HEK293 cells potentially reflecting differences in Piezo2/Mtmr2 stoichiometry or the contribution of unknown neuronal modulators.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and includes speculation about potential reasons for the difference from HEK293 cells.

claim: The inactivation time constant of RA-MA currents is unchanged upon Mtmr2 overexpression in DRG neurons.
source: Also, the inactivation time constant of RA-MA currents was unchanged upon overexpression of Mtmr2 in DRG neurons (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mtmr2 siRNA knockdown in DRG cultures results in successful reduction of Mtmr2 mRNA levels after 72 hours.
source: Successful knockdown of Mtmr2 was achieved after 72 hr and evaluated by quantitative PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Mtmr2 knockdown does not change Piezo2 mRNA levels in DRG cultures.
source: We assessed Piezo2 mRNA levels, Piezo2 membrane expression and the percentage of Piezo2-positive neurons and did not observe any changes upon Mtmr2 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Mtmr2 knockdown does not change Piezo2 membrane expression in DRG cultures.
source: We assessed Piezo2 mRNA levels, Piezo2 membrane expression and the percentage of Piezo2-positive neurons and did not observe any changes upon Mtmr2 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Mtmr2 knockdown does not change the percentage of Piezo2-positive neurons in DRG cultures.
source: We assessed Piezo2 mRNA levels, Piezo2 membrane expression and the percentage of Piezo2-positive neurons and did not observe any changes upon Mtmr2 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Mtmr2 siRNA knockdown significantly augments RA-MA current amplitude in DRG cultures.
source: However, when we measured RA-MA currents in Mtmr2 siRNA-nucleofected DRG cultures, we observed a significant augmentation in current amplitude whereas the displacement threshold and inactivation time constant were unchanged (Figure 2a–b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2a-b and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The displacement threshold of RA-MA currents remains unchanged upon Mtmr2 knockdown in DRG cultures.
source: However, when we measured RA-MA currents in Mtmr2 siRNA-nucleofected DRG cultures, we observed a significant augmentation in current amplitude whereas the displacement threshold and inactivation time constant were unchanged (Figure 2a–b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The inactivation time constant of RA-MA currents remains unchanged upon Mtmr2 knockdown in DRG cultures.
source: However, when we measured RA-MA currents in Mtmr2 siRNA-nucleofected DRG cultures, we observed a significant augmentation in current amplitude whereas the displacement threshold and inactivation time constant were unchanged (Figure 2a–b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: IA-MA currents are unaffected by Mtmr2 knockdown in DRG neurons.
source: These seemed to be largely unaltered by Mtmr2 knockdown (Figure 2c,d; Supplementary file 1) indicating that mechanotransduction is not generally compromised.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2c and Supplementary file 1.

claim: SA-MA currents are unaffected by Mtmr2 knockdown in DRG neurons.
source: These seemed to be largely unaltered by Mtmr2 knockdown (Figure 2c,d; Supplementary file 1) indicating that mechanotransduction is not generally compromised.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mtmr2 knockdown results in a significant redistribution of MA current subpopulations with an increase in RA-MA cells and a decrease in IA-MA cells.
source: Remarkably though, upon Mtmr2 knockdown we detected a significant redistribution of the number of cells exhibiting MA subpopulations: a moderate increase in the proportion of RA-MA cells paralleled by a decrease of the IA-MA population (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Mtmr2 catalyzes the removal of the 3-phosphate group from PI(3)P and PI(3,5)P2.
source: Functionally, Mtmr2 catalyzes the removal of a 3-phosphate group from its phosphoinositide (PIPs) substrates phosphatidylinositol 3-monophosphate PI(3)P and phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate PI(3,5)P2 (Begley et al., 2006; Berger et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Begley et al., 2006; Berger et al., 2002).

claim: PI(3,5)P2 is much less abundant than most other PIPs, for example PI(4,5)P2.
source: Remarkably, PI(3,5)P2 is much less abundant than most other PIPs, for example PI(4,5)P2 (Zolov et al., 2012), but can be rapidly and transiently regulated by a large enzymatic protein complex in response to cellular stimulation (McCartney et al., 2014a; Vaccari et al., 2011; Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Zolov et al., 2012).

claim: PI(3,5)P2 can be rapidly and transiently regulated by a large enzymatic protein complex in response to cellular stimulation.
source: Remarkably, PI(3,5)P2 is much less abundant than most other PIPs, for example PI(4,5)P2 (Zolov et al., 2012), but can be rapidly and transiently regulated by a large enzymatic protein complex in response to cellular stimulation (McCartney et al., 2014a; Vaccari et al., 2011; Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (McCartney et al., 2014a; Vaccari et al., 2011; Zolov et al., 2012).

claim: The catalytically inactive Mtmr2 C417S mutant does not suppress Piezo2-mediated currents in HEK293 cells.
source: This was indeed found to be the case. Mtmr2C417S co-expression did not suppress Piezo2-mediated currents in HEK293 cells as determined by comparison of stimulus-current curves (Figure 3a) with mock transfected cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Co-expression of catalytically inactive Mtmr2 C417S shows a trend towards moderate potentiation of Piezo2 currents, especially at low stimulus magnitudes.
source: Instead, we observed a trend towards moderate potentiation of Piezo2 currents upon co-expression of Mtmr2C417S (especially at low stimulus magnitudes; Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Enzymatically inactive Mtmr2 C417S remains capable of associating with Piezo2 in close proximity as shown by PLA.
source: Importantly, enzymatically inactive Mtmr2C417S was abundantly expressed and remained capable of associating with Piezo2 in close proximity as suggested by PLA upon co-overexpression of Piezo2 and Mtmr2C417S in comparison to wild type Mtmr2 (Figure 3b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 3b-c.

claim: Wortmannin application only marginally alters the increase in RA-MA currents upon Mtmr2 knockdown in neurons.
source: Wortmannin application only marginally altered the increase in RA-MA currents upon Mtmr2 knockdown in neurons (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Apilimod significantly diminishes the magnitude of RA-MA currents in Mtmr2 siRNA-treated neurons.
source: Apilimod, on the other hand, significantly diminished the magnitude of RA-MA currents in Mtmr2 siRNA-treated neurons (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The displacement threshold of RA-MA currents is significantly increased upon Apilimod treatment in Mtmr2 siRNA-treated neurons.
source: In line with a reversal of Mtmr2-induced potentiation, the displacement threshold of RA-MA currents was significantly increased upon Apilimod treatment (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Apilimod treatment in wild type DRG neurons does not affect RA-MA currents.
source: Interestingly, Apilimod treatment in wild type DRG neurons did not affect RA-MA currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b; Supplementary file 1), as expected given the low cellular expression and tight regulation of PI(3,5)P2 under physiological conditions (Jin et al., 2016; McCartney et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and Supplementary file 1, and citations to previous literature (Jin et al., 2016; McCartney et al., 2014a).

claim: Extracellular hypotonic stress counteracts the inhibition of Piezo2 RA-MA currents caused by Mtmr2 overexpression in DRG neurons.
source: Indeed, in Mtmr2 overexpressing DRG cultures we recorded significantly higher RA-MA currents under extracellular hypotonic conditions compared to isotonic conditions (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Intracellular hypotonic stress prevents RA-MA current sensitization upon Mtmr2 knockdown in DRG cultures.
source: As predicted, under intracellular hypotonic conditions RA-MA currents were significantly smaller in siRNA-treated cultures compared to isotonic conditions (Figure 4d; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mtmr2 knockdown does not alter the Young's elastic modulus of cultured DRG neurons as measured by AFM.
source: However, our experiments did not show any significant differences between Mtmr2 siRNA-treated and control-treated DRG neurons. Neither the Young´s elastic modulus (an indicator for cellular elasticity including membrane tension and cortex stiffness) (Morley et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2015) as determined from the indentation, nor the tether force (an indicator for membrane tension and mechanical coupling to the cortex) (Qi et al., 2015) obtained from the retraction portion of the force distance curves were altered (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mtmr2 knockdown does not alter the tether force of cultured DRG neurons as measured by AFM.
source: However, our experiments did not show any significant differences between Mtmr2 siRNA-treated and control-treated DRG neurons. Neither the Young´s elastic modulus (an indicator for cellular elasticity including membrane tension and cortex stiffness) (Morley et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2015) as determined from the indentation, nor the tether force (an indicator for membrane tension and mechanical coupling to the cortex) (Qi et al., 2015) obtained from the retraction portion of the force distance curves were altered (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Piezo2 contains a region with considerable similarity to the proposed PI(3,5)P2 binding motif of TRPML1.
source: Sequence analysis revealed a region in Piezo2 with considerable similarity to the proposed PI(3,5)P2 binding motif of the mucolipin TRP channel 1 (TRPML1) (Dong et al., 2010) (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5a and citation to previous literature (Dong et al., 2010).

claim: The Piezo2 peptide corresponding to the identified region binds to PI(3,5)P2 in a peptide-lipid binding assay.
source: We performed a peptide-lipid binding assay to test if this sequence in Piezo2 could bind to PI(3,5)P2, which was indeed the case (Figure 5b,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide-lipid binding assay data shown in Figure 5b,d.

claim: The Piezo2 peptide binds to PI(4,5)P2 in a peptide-lipid binding assay.
source: In addition, we also observed that the Piezo2 peptide was able to bind PI(4,5)P2 and weakly to PI(3,4)P2 (Figure 5b,d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide-lipid binding assay data shown in Figure 5b,d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Piezo2 peptide binds weakly to PI(3,4)P2 in a peptide-lipid binding assay.
source: In addition, we also observed that the Piezo2 peptide was able to bind PI(4,5)P2 and weakly to PI(3,4)P2 (Figure 5b,d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide-lipid binding assay data shown in Figure 5b,d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mutated Piezo2 3Q peptide does not bind to any lipid in a peptide-lipid binding assay.
source: In parallel we performed the binding assay with a mutated version of the Piezo2 peptide, in which positively-charged amino acid residues shown to be relevant for PI(3,5)P2 binding in TRPML1 were changed to neutral Glutamine (Q; Piezo2 3Q mutant; QQILQYFWMS). This mutated peptide did not bind to any lipid (Figure 5b,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide-lipid binding assay data shown in Figure 5b,d.

claim: The identified PI(3,5)P2-binding region in Piezo2 exhibits 50% sequence identity to Piezo1 with conservation of positively charged amino acid residues.
source: The here identified PI(3,5)P2-binding region in Piezo2 exhibits 50% sequence identity to Piezo1 with conservation of positively charged amino acid residues (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The Piezo1 peptide does not bind to PI(3,5)P2 in a peptide-lipid binding assay.
source: Therefore, we also tested whether Piezo1 was able to bind PI(3,5)P2, but did not find any evidence for this (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide-lipid binding assay data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: MA currents of the Piezo2 P1 mutant (with the PI(3,5)P2 binding domain swapped with Piezo1) are only slightly attenuated upon co-expression with Mtmr2 compared to mock controls.
source: Remarkably, MA currents of the Piezo2 P1 mutant were only slightly attenuated upon co-expression with Mtmr2 compared to mock-transfected controls (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The displacement threshold and inactivation time constant of MA currents of the Piezo2 P1 mutant remain unchanged upon Mtmr2 overexpression.
source: Also, the displacement threshold and inactivation time constant of MA currents remained unchanged (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Piezo2 ion channels are critical determinants of the sense of light touch in vertebrates.
source: Piezo2 ion channels are critical determinants of the sense of light touch in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Piezo2 ion channels mediate rapidly adapting mechanically activated (RA-MA) currents in sensory neurons of dorsal root ganglia (DRG).
source: Piezo2 ion channels have emerged as major somatosensory mechanotransducers and mediate rapidly adapting mechanically activated (RA-MA) currents in sensory neurons, such as those of dorsal root ganglia (DRG) (Coste et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Coste et al., 2010, 2012).

claim: Piezo2 is crucially involved in vertebrate light touch and proprioception.
source: By now it has been established that Piezo2 is crucially involved in vertebrate light touch and proprioception (Coste et al., 2010, 2012; Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2015; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Coste et al., 2010, 2012; Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2015; Woo et al., 2014).

claim: RA-MA currents are inhibited through depletion of PI(4,5)P2 and PI(4)P.
source: In case of Piezo2, RA-MA currents were shown to be inhibited through depletion of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) and phosphatidylinositol 4-monophosphate (PI(4)P) (Borbiro et al., 2015), and also by depletion of cholesterol at the plasma membrane (Qi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Borbiro et al., 2015).

claim: RA-MA currents are inhibited by depletion of cholesterol at the plasma membrane.
source: In case of Piezo2, RA-MA currents were shown to be inhibited through depletion of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) and phosphatidylinositol 4-monophosphate (PI(4)P) (Borbiro et al., 2015), and also by depletion of cholesterol at the plasma membrane (Qi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Qi et al., 2015).

claim: Lipid- or cytoskeleton-induced changes in plasma membrane tension impact somatosensory mechanotransduction.
source: Besides, lipid- or cytoskeleton-induced changes in plasma membrane tension have been shown to impact somatosensory mechanotransduction (Jia et al., 2016; Morley et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Jia et al., 2016; Morley et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2015).

claim: STOML3 is a protein-protein interaction partner relevant for Piezo2 physiology.
source: These include stomatin-like protein STOML3 (Poole et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2015; Wetzel et al., 2007), unidentified protein tethers to the extracellular matrix (Hu et al., 2010) and Pericentrin (Narayanan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Poole et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2015; Wetzel et al., 2007).

claim: Pericentrin is a protein-protein interaction partner relevant for Piezo2 physiology.
source: These include stomatin-like protein STOML3 (Poole et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2015; Wetzel et al., 2007), unidentified protein tethers to the extracellular matrix (Hu et al., 2010) and Pericentrin (Narayanan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Narayanan et al., 2016).

claim: Mtmr2 was previously described to be highly expressed in DRG sensory neurons and Schwann cells.
source: Interestingly, Mtmr2 was previously described to be highly expressed in DRG sensory neurons and Schwann cells (Bolino et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bolino et al., 2002).

claim: 20.37 ± 2.01% of DRG neurons exhibit positive Mtmr2 immunolabel.
source: 20.37 ± 2.01% of DRG neurons exhibit positive Mtmr2 immunolabel and 24.53 ± 1.21% of DRG neurons were positive for GFP indicating the presence of Piezo2.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: 24.53 ± 1.21% of DRG neurons are positive for GFP indicating the presence of Piezo2.
source: 20.37 ± 2.01% of DRG neurons exhibit positive Mtmr2 immunolabel and 24.53 ± 1.21% of DRG neurons were positive for GFP indicating the presence of Piezo2.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Among Piezo2-positive cells, 51.61 ± 3.71% cells are Mtmr2-positive.
source: Among Piezo2-positive cells, 51.61 ± 3.71% cells were found to be Mtmr2-positive.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Mtmr2 levels control Piezo2-mediated RA-MA currents.
source: Here, we show that Mtmr2 levels control Piezo2-mediated RA-MA currents.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Discussion that is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Elevated Mtmr2 expression attenuates Piezo2 RA-MA currents.
source: While elevated Mtmr2 expression attenuated Piezo2 RA-MA currents, siRNA-mediated knockdown of Mtmr2 resulted in Piezo2 RA-MA current potentiation.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Discussion that is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of Mtmr2 results in Piezo2 RA-MA current potentiation.
source: While elevated Mtmr2 expression attenuated Piezo2 RA-MA currents, siRNA-mediated knockdown of Mtmr2 resulted in Piezo2 RA-MA current potentiation.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Discussion that is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Mtmr2-dependent Piezo2 inhibition involves depletion of PI(3,5)P2.
source: Mechanistically, our experiments with catalytically inactive Mtmr2, pharmacological inhibitors, and osmotic stress suggest that changes in the levels of PI(3,5)P2 regulate Piezo2 RA-MA currents.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Discussion that is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The PI(3,5)P2 binding region in Piezo2 confers sensitivity to Mtmr2 as indicated by functional analysis of a domain-swapped Piezo2 mutant.
source: Further, we identified a PI(3,5)P2 binding region in Piezo2, but not Piezo1, that confers sensitivity to Mtmr2 as indicated by functional analysis of a domain-swapped Piezo2 mutant.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Abstract that is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Local PI(3,5)P2 modulation via Mtmr2 in the vicinity of Piezo2 is a novel mechanism to dynamically control Piezo2-dependent mechanotransduction in peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Altogether, our results propose local PI(3,5)P2 modulation via Mtmr2 in the vicinity of Piezo2 as a novel mechanism to dynamically control Piezo2-dependent mechanotransduction in peripheral sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Abstract that is supported by the experimental data and interpretations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mtmr2 attenuates Piezo2-mediated rapidly adapting mechanically activated (RA-MA) currents.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Mtmr2 attenuates Piezo2-mediated rapidly adapting mechanically activated (RA-MA) currents.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Abstract that is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Mtmr2 and its PIP substrates are implicated in Piezo2-mediated mechanotransduction.
source: Altogether, this raises the question whether Mtmr2 and its PIP substrates are implicated in Piezo2-mediated mechanotransduction and generally, in somatosensory mechanosensation.
evidence: This is a question posed in the Introduction that is addressed and supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The catalytic activity of Mtmr2 and the consequential alteration of PIP levels underlie the regulation of Piezo2 by Mtmr2.
source: This result strongly suggests that the catalytic activity of Mtmr2 and the consequential alteration of PIP levels (Laporte et al., 1998; McCartney et al., 2014b; Mironova et al., 2016; Previtali et al., 2007) may underlie the regulation of Piezo2 by Mtmr2.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data with the catalytically inactive Mtmr2 C417S mutant shown in Figure 3a, supported by citations to previous literature (Laporte et al., 1998; McCartney et al., 2014b; Mironova et al., 2016; Previtali et al., 2007).

claim: Hypoosmotic stress elevates PI(3,5)P2 levels in eukaryotic cells.
source: Upon hypoosmotic stress Mtmr2 trafficking was altered and PI(3,5)P2 levels were reported to be elevated in eukaryotic cells (Berger et al., 2003; Dove et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Berger et al., 2003; Dove et al., 1997).

claim: Hypoosmotic stress potentiates Piezo2 RA-MA currents independent of TRPV4.
source: In the case of Piezo2, hypoosmotic stress was shown to potentiate Piezo2 RA-MA currents, which was independent of the prominent osmosensor TRPV4 (Jia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Jia et al., 2016).

claim: Extracellular hypotonic stress potentiates Piezo2 RA-MA currents in DRG cultures.
source: First, we confirmed the previously described (Jia et al., 2016) potentiation of Piezo2 RA-MA currents by application of extracellular hypotonic stress to DRG cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and citation to previous literature (Jia et al., 2016).

claim: Mtmr13 and Mtmr2 reciprocally control their abundance at the membrane of cultured cell lines.
source: For example, Mtmr13 and Mtmr2 reciprocally control their abundance at the membrane of cultured cell lines (Ng et al., 2013; Robinson and Dixon, 2005) and in uncharacterized endomembrane compartments in Schwann cells (Ng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Ng et al., 2013; Robinson and Dixon, 2005).

claim: Mtmr2 enzymatic activity is augmented through interaction with Mtmr13.
source: In addition, Mtmr2 enzymatic activity is augmented through interaction with Mtmr13 (Berger et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Berger et al., 2006).

claim: Mtmr1 and Mtmr5 were identified as additional members of the Piezo2 interactome.
source: In this respect it is noteworthy that our interactomics screen (Narayanan et al., 2016) identified two additional Mtmr family members: Mtmr1 and Mtmr5.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the previous interactomics screen (Narayanan et al., 2016).

claim: Mtmr1 is similar to Mtmr2 in structure and substrate specificity.
source: Mtmr1 was shown to be similar to Mtmr2 in structure and substrate specificity (Bong et al., 2016), but is much less studied than Mtmr2.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bong et al., 2016).

claim: Mtmr5 is a catalytically inactive phosphatase which binds to Mtmr2, increases its enzymatic activity and controls its subcellular localization.
source: Mtmr5 is a catalytically inactive phosphatase which binds to Mtmr2, increases its enzymatic activity and controls its subcellular localization (Kim et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kim et al., 2003).

claim: A multiprotein complex of different Mtmr family members might affect Piezo2 function.
source: The fact that Mtmr5 was previously reported as a binding partner of Mtmr2 further validates our published interactomics data (Narayanan et al., 2016), and hints towards the intriguing possibility that a multiprotein complex of different Mtmr family members might affect Piezo2 function.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the identification of multiple Mtmr family members in the Piezo2 interactome and known interactions between Mtmr family members.

claim: Enzymatic activity of Mtmr2 and consequently PI(3,5)P2 availability modulates Piezo2 RA-MA currents.
source: Mechanistically, our in vitro data strongly suggest that enzymatic activity of Mtmr2 and consequently PI(3,5)P2 availability modulates Piezo2 RA-MA currents.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the Discussion that is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Mtmr2 activity usually serves a dual function: dephosphorylation of PI(3,5)P2 and of PI(3)P, albeit the latter with lower efficiency.
source: Here, it is important to note that Mtmr2 activity usually serves a dual function: dephosphorylation of PI(3,5)P2 and of PI(3)P, albeit the latter with lower efficiency (Berger et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Berger et al., 2002).

claim: Wortmannin is commonly used to block class III PI 3-kinase but also inhibits class I PI 3-kinase.
source: Wortmannin is commonly used to block class III PI 3-kinase (please see scheme in Figure 4a), however, it also is reported to inhibit class I PI 3-kinase (Messenger et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Messenger et al., 2015).

claim: Previous work on Mtmr2 has shown only minor modifications of PI(3)P levels in Mtmr2-deficient cells.
source: Biologically, many enzymes control PI(3)P synthesis (Yan and Backer, 2007; Zolov et al., 2012) and previous work on Mtmr2 has only shown minor modifications of PI(3)P levels in Mtmr2-deficient cells (Cao et al., 2008; Vaccari et al., 2011) in line with its substrate preference (Berger et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Cao et al., 2008; Vaccari et al., 2011; Berger et al., 2002).

claim: The identified PI(3,5)P2-binding region is conserved among Piezo2 in vertebrates.
source: Interestingly, the here identified PI(3,5)P2-binding region is conserved among Piezo2 in vertebrates and exhibits 50% of sequence identity to mouse Piezo1 with conservation of basic amino acid residues.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison across species.

claim: Arthropods and nematodes, which only encode one Piezo protein, exhibit lower sequence similarity in the PI(3,5)P2-binding region: 40% (D. melanogaster) and 30% (C. elegans).
source: Arthropods and nematodes, which only encode one Piezo protein, exhibit lower sequence similarity in this region, 40% (D. melanogaster) and 30% (C. elegans), respectively.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison across species.

claim: PI(3,5)P2 was believed to predominantly act in the endo-lysosome system of eukaryotes.
source: PI(3,5)P2 was believed to predominantly act in the endo-lysosome system of eukaryotes (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006; Dong et al., 2010; Ho et al., 2012; Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006; Dong et al., 2010; Ho et al., 2012; Zolov et al., 2012).

claim: PI(3,5)P2 can serve a diverse range of cellular functions, such as autophagy, signaling in response to stress, control of membrane traffic to the plasma membrane as well as regulation of receptors and ion channels.
source: By now the picture is emerging that PI(3,5)P2 can serve a diverse range of cellular functions, such as autophagy, signaling in response to stress, control of membrane traffic to the plasma membrane as well as regulation of receptors and ion channels (Dong et al., 2010; Ho et al., 2012; Ikonomov et al., 2007; Klaus et al., 2009; McCartney et al., 2014b; Tsuruta et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Dong et al., 2010; Ho et al., 2012; Ikonomov et al., 2007; Klaus et al., 2009; McCartney et al., 2014b; Tsuruta et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: PI(3,5)P2 synthesis and metabolism are dynamically regulated and subject to cellular stimulation and stressors.
source: Moreover, depending on the cell type, PI(3,5)P2 synthesis and metabolism are dynamically regulated and subject to cellular stimulation and stressors, for example insulin-mediated PI(3,5)P2 changes in adipocytes (Ikonomov et al., 2007), neuronal activity-dependent synthesis at hippocampal synapses (McCartney et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012) and the here exploited regulation of PI(3,5)P2 upon osmotic shock in mammalian cell lines (Dove et al., 1997; Nicot and Laporte, 2008; Previtali et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Ikonomov et al., 2007; McCartney et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012; Dove et al., 1997; Nicot and Laporte, 2008; Previtali et al., 2007).

claim: PI(3,5)P2 synthesis and turnover is confined to membrane microdomains.
source: Instead of acting in a cell-wide manner, PI(3,5)P2 synthesis and turnover is confined to membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about PI(3,5)P2 regulation.

claim: PI(3,5)P2 microdomains ensure dynamic and local control of PI(3,5)P2 levels.
source: Despite their unknown composition and subcellular localization, these microdomains are believed to ensure dynamic and local control of PI(3,5)P2 levels (Ho et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2016; McCartney et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Ho et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2016; McCartney et al., 2014a).

claim: Mtmr2 may physically bind to Piezo2 to ensure its enrichment in PI(3,5)P2 microdomains.
source: Mtmr2 may physically bind to Piezo2 in order to ensure its enrichment in PI(3,5)P2 microdomains, so that local PI(3,5)P2 changes or yet to be identified effector proteins can efficiently modulate Piezo2 (Figure 6, working model).
evidence: This is a proposed working model based on the experimental data and known properties of PI(3,5)P2 microdomains, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: A physical interaction between Mtmr2 and Piezo2 would selectively concentrate Piezo2 at the sites of PI(3,5)P2 depletion thereby allowing its inhibition in a defined membrane compartment.
source: In these microdomains Mtmr2 would catalytically decrease PI(3,5)P2 levels, which in turn could inhibit Piezo2 function. Hence, a physical interaction between Mtmr2 and Piezo2 would selectively concentrate Piezo2 at the sites of PI(3,5)P2 depletion thereby allowing its inhibition in a defined membrane compartment.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and known properties of PI(3,5)P2 microdomains.

claim: Reduced Mtmr2 expression or activity would increase local PI(3,5)P2 levels and facilitate Piezo2 potentiation.
source: On the contrary, reduced Mtmr2 expression or activity would be expected to increase local PI(3,5)P2 levels (Laporte et al., 1998; McCartney et al., 2014b; Mironova et al., 2016; Previtali et al., 2007; Vaccari et al., 2011) and facilitate Piezo2 potentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to previous literature (Laporte et al., 1998; McCartney et al., 2014b; Mironova et al., 2016; Previtali et al., 2007; Vaccari et al., 2011).

claim: Mtmr2-controlled PI(3,5)P2 availability could cause local changes in membrane tension.
source: It is conceivable that Mtmr2-controlled PI(3,5)P2 availability could in turn cause local changes in membrane tension (Lewis and Grandl, 2015; Perozo et al., 2002; Vásquez et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on known effects of lipids on membrane tension, supported by citations to previous literature (Lewis and Grandl, 2015; Perozo et al., 2002; Vásquez et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2017).

claim: Local membrane tension has been demonstrated to affect Piezo1 MA currents.
source: The latter has already been demonstrated to affect Piezo1 MA currents (Cox et al., 2016; Lewis and Grandl, 2015; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Cox et al., 2016; Lewis and Grandl, 2015; Wu et al., 2016).

claim: AMPA receptor abundance at hippocampal synapses is regulated by PI(3,5)P2-controlled cycling through early and late endosomes.
source: Along these lines it is worth mentioning that AMPA receptor abundance at hippocampal synapses has been shown to be regulated by PI(3,5)P2-controlled cycling through early and late endosomes (McCartney et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (McCartney et al., 2014b).

claim: Piezo1 has been described to reside in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: While unknown so far, localization of Piezo2 to intracellular membranes would not be unexpected (Coste et al., 2010) since its family member Piezo1 has originally been described to reside in the endoplasmic reticulum (McHugh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (McHugh et al., 2010).

claim: Multiple Mtmr2 mutations have been implicated in Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 4B1 (CMT4B1) disease.
source: In this respect it is noteworthy that multiple Mtmr2 mutations – including those affecting its activity (Berger et al., 2002) – have been implicated in Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 4B1 (CMT4B1) disease, a peripheral neuropathy characterized by abnormalities in myelination and nerve conduction (Bolino et al., 2004; Bolis et al., 2005; Bonneick et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Berger et al., 2002; Bolino et al., 2004; Bolis et al., 2005; Bonneick et al., 2005).

claim: CMT4B1 disease is a peripheral neuropathy characterized by abnormalities in myelination and nerve conduction.
source: In this respect it is noteworthy that multiple Mtmr2 mutations – including those affecting its activity (Berger et al., 2002) – have been implicated in Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 4B1 (CMT4B1) disease, a peripheral neuropathy characterized by abnormalities in myelination and nerve conduction (Bolino et al., 2004; Bolis et al., 2005; Bonneick et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bolino et al., 2004; Bolis et al., 2005; Bonneick et al., 2005).

claim: PI(3,5)P2 is 125-fold less abundant than PI(4,5)P2 in mammalian cells.
source: PI(3,5)P2 is much less abundant than most PIPs, for example 125-fold less than PI(4,5)P2 in mammalian cells (Zolov et al., 2012), and tightly regulated by a large protein complex (Vaccari et al., 2011; Zolov et al., 2012) (please see scheme in Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Zolov et al., 2012).

claim: PI(3,5)P2 is tightly regulated by a large protein complex.
source: PI(3,5)P2 is much less abundant than most PIPs, for example 125-fold less than PI(4,5)P2 in mammalian cells (Zolov et al., 2012), and tightly regulated by a large protein complex (Vaccari et al., 2011; Zolov et al., 2012) (please see scheme in Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Vaccari et al., 2011; Zolov et al., 2012) and illustrated in Figure 4a.
